topic: Trading, returns, settlement and corporate actions

notes.front: What is a market order?
notes.back: An order to buy or sell at the best available price; it generally executes immediately, but the price is not guaranteed.
notes.explanation: It trades certainty of execution for uncertainty of price.
notes.example: Like telling a shop “I’ll take it at whatever the till says”, but for shares.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC), Investor Bulletin “Understanding Order Types” (updated 18 August 2026), “Market Order”
notes.evidence: A market order is an order to buy or sell a stock at the best available price. Generally, a market order will be executed immediately. However, the price at which a market order will be executed is not guaranteed.

notes.front: What is a limit order?
notes.back: An order to buy or sell at a specific price or better.
notes.explanation: A buy limit can fill only at the limit or lower, and a sell limit only at the limit or higher.
notes.example: Like telling an estate agent you will pay no more than $300,000 for a house, but for shares.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC), Investor Bulletin “Understanding Order Types” (updated 18 August 2026), “Limit Order”
notes.evidence: A limit order is an order to buy or sell a stock at a specific price or better. A buy limit order can only be executed at the limit price or lower, and a sell limit order can only be executed at the limit price or higher.

notes.front: What is a stop order?
notes.back: An order that becomes a market order once the stock reaches a set price, the stop price.
notes.explanation: Until the stop price is reached the order does nothing; after that it behaves like any market order.
notes.example: Like a smoke alarm that stays silent until a set level, then acts at once, but for a trade.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC), Investor Bulletin “Stop, Stop-Limit, and Trailing Stop Orders” (updated 18 August 2026), “Stop Order”
notes.evidence: A stop order, also referred to as a stop-loss order, is an order to buy or sell a stock once the price of the stock reaches a specified price, known as the stop price. When the stop price is reached, a stop order becomes a market order .

notes.front: What is a stop-limit order?
notes.back: An order that becomes a limit order once the stop price is reached, executing only at the limit price or better.
notes.explanation: It combines a stop order and a limit order, which lets the investor control the price at which it can execute.
notes.example: Like a stop order with a floor: once triggered, it still refuses any price worse than the one you set.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC), Investor Bulletin “Stop, Stop-Limit, and Trailing Stop Orders” (updated 18 August 2026), “Stop-Limit Order”
notes.evidence: A stop-limit order is an order to buy or sell a stock that combines the features of a stop order and a limit order . Once the stop price is reached, a stop-limit order becomes a limit order that will be executed at a specified price (or better).

notes.front: What is a day order?
notes.back: An order good only during the trading day it is entered; it is the default when no time frame is given.
notes.explanation: Unless the investor says otherwise, an order lasts only for the day it is entered.
notes.example: Like a same-day offer that lapses at closing time if nobody accepts it.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC), Investor Bulletin “Understanding Order Types” (updated 18 August 2026), “Day”
notes.evidence: Unless an investor specifies a time frame for the expiration of an order, orders to buy and sell a stock are “Day” orders, meaning they are good only during the trading day that the order is entered.

notes.front: What is a good-til-canceled (GTC) order?
notes.back: An order that lasts until it is executed in full or cancelled.
notes.explanation: Unlike a day order, it does not lapse at the end of the trading day.
notes.example: Like a standing offer on a house that stays open until the seller accepts or you withdraw it.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC), Investor Bulletin “Understanding Order Types” (updated 18 August 2026), “Good-Til-Canceled (GTC)”
notes.evidence: A GTC order is an order to buy or sell a stock that lasts until it is executed in full or it is canceled.

notes.front: What is a discretionary order?
notes.back: An order the firm or its associated person enters by exercising discretionary authority over the customer’s account.
notes.explanation: SEC record-keeping rules require such orders to be marked as discretionary on the order record.
notes.example: Like a trusted agent buying on your behalf without asking first, but in a brokerage account you have authorised.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.17a-3 (Rule 17a-3, records to be made by certain exchange members, brokers and dealers), eCFR, paragraph (a)(6)
notes.evidence: An order entered pursuant to the exercise of discretionary authority by the member, broker or dealer, or associated person thereof, must be so designated.

notes.front: What is the bid?
notes.back: The highest price a buyer will pay for a specified number of shares at a given time.
notes.explanation: It is the buyers’ side of a quote, so a seller looks to it.
notes.example: Like the best offer a dealer will pay for your used car today.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Bid Price”
notes.evidence: The term "bid" refers to the highest price a buyer will pay to buy a specified number of shares of a stock at any given time.

notes.front: What is the ask (offer)?
notes.back: The lowest price at which a seller will sell the stock.
notes.explanation: It is the sellers’ side of a quote, so a buyer looks to it.
notes.example: Like the lowest price on the dealer’s forecourt sign for a car you want to buy.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Bid Price”
notes.evidence: The term ask refers to the lowest price at which a seller will sell the stock.

notes.front: What is the spread?
notes.back: The difference between the bid price and the ask price.
notes.explanation: Because the bid is almost always below the ask, there is normally a gap between the two.
notes.example: Like the gap between what a currency booth pays for dollars and what it charges for them.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Bid Price”
notes.evidence: The bid price will almost always be lower than the ask or “offer,” price. The difference between the bid price and the ask price is called the "spread."

notes.front: When does a broker-dealer act in a principal capacity?
notes.back: When it buys from or sells to you directly from its own inventory.
notes.explanation: The firm is the other side of your trade rather than finding one for you.
notes.example: Like a bookshop selling you a book from its own shelves, rather than ordering it from someone else for a fee.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Markups and Markdowns”
notes.evidence: When a broker-dealer buys from or sells to you directly securities it holds in its own inventory, the broker-dealer acts as a principal in the transaction.

notes.front: What is agency capacity, and how is the firm paid in it?
notes.back: The firm acts as your agent in the transaction and is paid a commission.
notes.explanation: As agent the firm arranges the trade for you rather than trading from its own account.
notes.example: Like an estate agent who finds a buyer for your house and charges a fee.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Commissions”
notes.evidence: The commission compensates the financial professional and his or her firm when it is acting as agent for you in your securities transaction.

notes.front: What is a markup?
notes.back: The amount above the market price a broker-dealer acting as principal charges when selling to you.
notes.explanation: A principal is generally paid through its price, not a separate fee.
notes.example: Like a shop adding its margin to what it paid for goods, but for a bond from the firm’s inventory.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Markups and Markdowns”
notes.evidence: When acting as a principal, the broker-dealer generally will be compensated by selling the security to you at a price that is higher than the market price (the difference is called a markup)

notes.front: What is a commission?
notes.back: The charge that pays the professional and firm for acting as your agent when you buy or sell securities.
notes.explanation: It pays the firm for arranging the trade on your behalf as your agent.
notes.example: Like the fee an auction house charges for selling your painting.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Commissions”
notes.evidence: The commission compensates the financial professional and his or her firm when it is acting as agent for you in your securities transaction.

notes.front: What is a long position?
notes.back: Owning the security, expecting it to rise in value.
notes.explanation: Its opposite is a short position.
notes.example: Like buying a painting you expect to be worth more next year.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC), “Stock Purchases and Sales: Long and Short”
notes.evidence: Having a “long” position in a security means that you own the security. Investors maintain “long” security positions in the expectation that the stock will rise in value in the future.

notes.front: What is a short sale, as the SEC’s short-sale rules define it?
notes.back: A sale of a security the seller does not own, or one completed by delivering a borrowed security.
notes.explanation: The definition covers both parts: selling what you do not own, and settling that sale with borrowed securities.
notes.example: Like selling a friend’s borrowed book now, planning to buy a copy later to give back.
notes.source: 17 CFR 242.200 (Rule 200 of the SEC short-sale rules, definition of short sale), eCFR, paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: The term short sale shall mean any sale of a security which the seller does not own or any sale which is consummated by the delivery of a security borrowed by, or for the account of, the seller.

notes.front: What does it mean to be bullish?
notes.back: Expecting prices to rise; a bull market is a time of rising prices and optimism.
notes.explanation: Investor.gov defines a bull market as a time of rising prices and optimism; being bullish means expecting such a rise.
notes.example: Like a homeowner confident local house prices will keep climbing.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Bull Market”
notes.evidence: A time when stock prices are rising and market sentiment is optimistic.

notes.front: What does it mean to be bearish?
notes.back: Expecting prices to fall; a bear market is a time of falling prices and pessimism.
notes.explanation: Investor.gov defines a bear market as a time of falling prices and pessimism; being bearish means expecting such a fall.
notes.example: Like a homeowner who expects local house prices to slide.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Bear Market”
notes.evidence: A time when stock prices are declining and market sentiment is pessimistic.

notes.front: What is a return of capital?
notes.back: A distribution that gives back some or all of your investment in the company; it is not a dividend.
notes.explanation: Because it hands back your own investment, it lowers your cost basis rather than counting as a dividend.
notes.example: Like a friend repaying part of the money you put into their business, rather than paying you a share of profits.
notes.source: IRS, Topic no. 404, Dividends and other corporate distributions, “Return of capital (nondividend and liquidating distributions)”
notes.evidence: Distributions that qualify as a return of capital aren't dividends. A return of capital is a return of some or all of your investment in the stock of the company. A return of capital reduces the adjusted cost basis of your stock.

notes.front: What is a realized gain?
notes.back: The gain fixed when you sell an asset: the amount realized from the sale above its adjusted basis.
notes.explanation: The sale is what turns a price rise into a capital gain or loss for tax purposes.
notes.example: Like selling a car for more than you paid: the profit is locked in once the buyer pays.
notes.source: IRS, Topic no. 409, Capital gains and losses, “Capital gains and losses”
notes.evidence: When you sell a capital asset, the difference between the adjusted basis in the asset and the amount you realized from the sale is a capital gain or a capital loss.

notes.front: What is an unrealized gain?
notes.back: A profit on a position you still hold open, not yet sold.
notes.explanation: A capital gain is fixed only when you sell; Publication 550 uses “unrealized profit” for futures contracts still open at year end.
notes.example: Like a house that has risen in value while you still live in it.
notes.source: IRS, Publication 550, Investment Income and Expenses, chapter 4, Form 1099-B and regulated futures contracts
notes.evidence: had unrealized profit or loss on these contracts that were open at the end of 2024 or 2025

notes.front: What is a cash dividend?
notes.back: A distribution of a corporation’s earnings and profits paid to shareholders in cash, the most common form.
notes.explanation: Dividends are paid out of earnings and profits, and corporations pay most of them in cash.
notes.example: Like a co-operative sharing out part of its yearly profit to members as cash.
notes.source: IRS, Topic no. 404, Dividends and other corporate distributions, Dividends
notes.evidence: Dividends are distributions of earnings and profits a corporation may pay you if you own stock in that corporation. Corporations pay most dividends in cash.

notes.front: What is a stock dividend?
notes.back: A distribution by a corporation of its own stock to its shareholders.
notes.explanation: Instead of cash, holders receive more shares, and generally such dividends are not taxable when received.
notes.example: Like a club giving members extra membership units instead of a cash payout.
notes.source: IRS, Publication 550, Investment Income and Expenses, chapter 1, “Distributions of Stock and Stock Rights”
notes.evidence: Distributions by a corporation of its own stock are commonly known as stock dividends. Stock rights (known as “stock options”) are distributions by a corporation of rights to acquire the corporation's stock. Generally, stock dividends and stock rights are not taxable to you, and you do not report them on your return.

notes.front: What is the record date?
notes.back: The date by which you must be on the company’s books as a shareholder to receive a declared dividend.
notes.explanation: The company sets it when it declares a dividend, and uses it to decide who gets the payment.
notes.example: Like the cut-off date on a club register for who receives this year’s members’ gift.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Ex-Dividend Dates: When Are You Entitled to Stock and Cash Dividends”
notes.evidence: When a company declares a dividend, it sets a record date when you must be on the company's books as a shareholder to receive the dividend.

notes.front: What is the ex-dividend date?
notes.back: The date from which a buyer of the stock no longer receives the next dividend.
notes.explanation: It is usually the record date itself, or one business day earlier if the record date is not a business day.
notes.example: Like the day a raffle closes: tickets bought from then on miss this draw.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Ex-Dividend Dates: When Are You Entitled to Stock and Cash Dividends”
notes.evidence: The ex-dividend date for stocks is usually set as the record date or one business day before if the record date is not a business day. If you purchase a stock on its ex-dividend date or after, you will not receive the next dividend payment.

notes.front: What is the payable date?
notes.back: The date the declared dividend is actually paid to shareholders.
notes.explanation: It is fixed when the company declares the dividend.
notes.example: Like payday on a payslip, as opposed to the date your hours were counted.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Ex-Dividend Dates: When Are You Entitled to Stock and Cash Dividends”, Example 1
notes.evidence: On March 2, 2026, Company XYZ declares a dividend payable on March 17, 2026, to its shareholders.

notes.front: What is yield to maturity (YTM)?
notes.back: The annual return on a bond held to maturity, given when you bought it and what you paid.
notes.explanation: Because it reflects the price paid, not just the coupon, it is widely used to compare bonds.
notes.example: Like working out the true yearly return on a loan you bought second-hand at a discount.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC), Investor Bulletin “What Are Corporate Bonds?”, basic financial terms of a corporate bond
notes.evidence: Yield to maturity is a widely used measure to compare bonds. This is the annual return on the bond if held to maturity taking into account when you bought the bond and what you paid for it.

notes.front: What is yield to call (YTC)?
notes.back: A bond yield figured to a call date and call price rather than to maturity.
notes.explanation: Rule 10b-10 lists yield to call beside yield to maturity, and a trade done at yield to call must also show the type of call, the call date and the call price.
notes.example: Like judging a loan’s return on the assumption the borrower repays on the first allowed early date.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.10b-10 (Rule 10b-10, confirmation of transactions), eCFR, paragraph (a)(6)(i)
notes.evidence: The yield at which the transaction was effected, including the percentage amount and its characterization (e.g., current yield, yield to maturity, or yield to call) and if effected at yield to call, the type of call, the call date and call price

notes.front: What is a basis point (bp)?
notes.back: One one-hundredth of a percentage point (0.01%).
notes.explanation: Small yield and rate moves are quoted this way: eight percent equals 800 basis points.
notes.example: Like measuring in pennies rather than pounds, but for percentages.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Basis Point”
notes.evidence: One one-hundredth (.01) of a percentage point. For example, eight percent is equal to 800 basis points.

notes.front: What is the cost basis of stocks or bonds you buy?
notes.back: The purchase price plus costs such as commissions and recording or transfer fees.
notes.explanation: Costs of buying, such as commissions, are added to the price rather than ignored.
notes.example: Like the total you paid for a car including the dealer’s fees, not just the sticker price.
notes.source: IRS, Topic no. 703, Basis of assets, Basis of assets
notes.evidence: If you buy stocks or bonds, your basis is the purchase price plus any additional costs such as commissions and recording or transfer fees.

notes.front: What is a market index?
notes.back: A measure tracking the performance of a basket of stocks representing a market or sector.
notes.explanation: A chosen set of stocks stands in for a whole market or sector.
notes.example: Like a shopping-basket price index, but for a set of shares.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Market Indices”
notes.evidence: A market index tracks the performance of a specific "basket" of stocks that represent a particular market or economic sector.

notes.front: What is the trade date (T)?
notes.back: The date the contract to buy or sell is made; settlement deadlines count from it.
notes.explanation: SEC Rule 15c6-1 measures the settlement deadline in business days after the date of the contract.
notes.example: Like the day you sign to buy a car, before the money and keys change hands.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.15c6-1 (Rule 15c6-1, settlement cycle), eCFR, paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: provides for payment of funds and delivery of securities later than the first business day after the date of the contract

notes.front: What happens on the settlement date?
notes.back: Payment of funds and delivery of the securities complete the trade.
notes.explanation: SEC Rule 15c6-1 limits how long after the trade date payment and delivery may come.
notes.example: Like completion day on a house purchase, when money and keys change hands.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.15c6-1 (Rule 15c6-1, settlement cycle), eCFR, paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: a broker or dealer shall not effect or enter into a contract for the purchase or sale of a security (other than an exempted security, a government security, a municipal security, commercial paper, bankers' acceptances, or commercial bills) that provides for payment of funds and delivery of securities

notes.front: What is book-entry ownership?
notes.back: Holding securities as a record of ownership, with no paper certificate.
notes.explanation: Book-entry approaches remove the need to hold certificates, unlike the certificate form.
notes.example: Like an online bank balance instead of banknotes in a drawer.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Holding Your Securities”
notes.evidence: Alternative approaches eliminate the need to hold certificates by relying on a “book-entry” record of ownership.

notes.front: What does holding securities in street name mean?
notes.back: Your positions are recorded on your brokerage firm’s books, not in your own name on the company’s books.
notes.explanation: It is one form of book-entry holding; direct registration is another.
notes.example: Like a cloakroom ticket: the attendant holds the coat, but it is yours.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Holding Your Securities”
notes.evidence: For example, you can hold your securities in “street name” where your securities positions are recorded on the books of your brokerage firm. Another book-entry option is direct registration where your securities positions are registered on the company's books.

notes.front: What is a stock split?
notes.back: An increase in the number of a company’s shares without any change in shareholders’ equity.
notes.explanation: Companies often split to make shares more affordable; the company’s value is simply cut into more pieces.
notes.example: Like cutting a pizza into 16 slices instead of 8: more slices, same pizza.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Stock Split”
notes.evidence: An increase in the number of shares of a corporation's stock without a change in the shareholders' equity. Companies often split shares of their stock to make them more affordable to investors.

notes.front: What is a reverse stock split?
notes.back: Each outstanding share is converted into a fraction of a share, cutting the number of shares.
notes.explanation: It is the opposite of a forward split: holders end up with fewer shares.
notes.example: Like swapping ten small coins for one larger one of the same total value.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Reverse Stock Splits”
notes.evidence: When a company completes a reverse stock split, each outstanding share of the company is converted into a fraction of a share.

notes.front: What is a stock buyback?
notes.back: An issuer repurchasing its own common stock, for example in the market.
notes.explanation: SEC Rule 10b-18 offers a safe harbour for such repurchases when they meet its conditions.
notes.example: Like a family firm buying back shares from outside owners.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.10b-18 (Rule 10b-18, purchases of certain equity securities by the issuer and others), eCFR, Preliminary note 1
notes.evidence: when they repurchase the issuer's common stock in the market in accordance with the section's manner, timing, price, and volume conditions

notes.front: What is a tender offer?
notes.back: A broad solicitation by a company or third party to buy a substantial percentage of a company’s securities.
notes.explanation: The bidder may be the company itself or a third party.
notes.example: Like a public offer to buy a large share of every member’s holding in a co-op, at a set price for a set time.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Tender Offer”
notes.evidence: A tender offer is typically an active and widespread solicitation by a company or third party (often called the “bidder” or “offeror”) to purchase a substantial percentage of the company’s securities.

notes.front: What is an exchange offer?
notes.back: A tender offer in which the offeror gives securities, registered with the SEC, for the securities tendered.
notes.explanation: Because securities are offered, a registration statement is involved, which Rule 162 addresses.
notes.example: Like offering your own club’s shares, not cash, to members of another club who hand in theirs.
notes.source: 17 CFR 230.162 (Rule 162, submission of tenders in registered exchange offers), eCFR, paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: an offeror may solicit tenders of securities in an exchange offer before a registration statement is effective as to the security offered

notes.front: What does a shareholder receive in a rights offering?
notes.back: Rights distributed by the corporation to acquire more of its stock.
notes.explanation: IRS guidance describes stock rights as distributions by a corporation of rights to acquire the corporation’s stock.
notes.example: Like a club giving each member the right to buy extra memberships at a set price.
notes.source: IRS, Publication 550, Investment Income and Expenses, chapter 1, “Distributions of Stock and Stock Rights”
notes.evidence: Stock rights (known as “stock options”) are distributions by a corporation of rights to acquire the corporation's stock.

notes.front: What is a merger, in mergers and acquisitions (M&A)?
notes.back: A transaction combining generally two or more companies into a single entity.
notes.explanation: Whether shareholders must approve it is governed by state law.
notes.example: Like two neighbouring shops joining into one business under one owner.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Mergers”
notes.evidence: Mergers are transactions involving the combination of generally two or more companies into a single entity. The need for shareholder approval of a merger is governed by state law.

notes.front: What is proxy voting?
notes.back: A way for shareholders to vote on directors and other matters without attending the meeting.
notes.explanation: The proxy lets a shareholder’s vote count even when they are absent.
notes.example: Like a postal vote in an election, but for a company meeting.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Proxy Voting”
notes.evidence: A way for shareholders to vote for corporate directors and on other matters affecting the company without having to personally attend the meeting.

notes.front: What is a proxy statement?
notes.back: A document telling shareholders when and where a meeting is and detailing the matters to be voted on.
notes.explanation: It gives shareholders what they need to vote in person or by proxy.
notes.example: Like the agenda and papers sent out before a club’s annual general meeting.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Proxy Statements”
notes.evidence: A document sent to shareholders letting them know when and where a shareholders’ meeting is taking place and detailing the matters to be voted upon at the meeting.

notes.front: Unless you specify otherwise, your broker will enter your order as a {{c1::market order}}.
notes.explanation: That default favours execution: with willing buyers and sellers, a market order is almost always filled.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Market Order”
notes.evidence: Unless you specify otherwise, your broker will enter your order as a market order. The advantage of a market order is that as long as there are willing buyers and sellers, you are almost always guaranteed your order will be executed.

notes.front: Is the last-traded price the price your market order will get?
notes.back: Not necessarily; the fill often differs from the last trade or real-time quote.
notes.explanation: Demand for the stock and the prices of available liquidity at the moment of execution decide the fill.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC), Investor Bulletin “Understanding Order Types” (updated 18 August 2026), “Market Order”
notes.evidence: The price at which a market order will execute often deviates from the last-traded price or “real time” quote due to the demand for a stock and the prices of available liquidity at the time of execution.

notes.front: Sam enters a market order to sell 200 shares. Near which quoted price will it generally execute?
notes.back: A: at or near the current bid.
notes.choices:
A) The current bid
B) The current ask
C) His own chosen price
notes.choicesExplained: B: a buy market order executes near the ask. C: a market order sets no price; that is a limit order.
notes.explanation: A seller trades with the buyers, whose best price is the bid.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC), “Types of Orders”
notes.evidence: A market order generally will execute at or near the current bid (for a sell order) or ask (for a buy order) price.

notes.front: Priya wants to buy shares of a company but will pay no more than $40. Which order fits?
notes.back: A: a buy limit order at $40.
notes.choices:
A) A buy limit order at $40
B) A buy stop order at $40
C) A market order
notes.choicesExplained: B: a buy stop becomes a market order at $40, with no cap on the price paid. C: a market order guarantees no price.
notes.explanation: A buy limit order can only be executed at the limit price or lower.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC), Investor Bulletin “Understanding Order Types” (updated 18 August 2026), “Limit Order”
notes.evidence: A buy limit order can only be executed at the limit price or lower, and a sell limit order can only be executed at the limit price or higher.

notes.front: What is the trade-off in using a limit order?
notes.back: It is not guaranteed to execute, but it ensures you do not pay more than your set price.
notes.explanation: It can only be filled if the market price reaches the limit, so the price protection costs certainty of execution.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC), Investor Bulletin “Understanding Order Types” (updated 18 August 2026), “Limit Order”
notes.evidence: A limit order is not guaranteed to execute. A limit order can only be filled if the stock’s market price reaches the limit price. While limit orders do not guarantee execution, they do help ensure that an investor does not pay more than a pre-determined price for a stock.

notes.front: A buy stop order is entered at a stop price {{c1::above}} the current market price.
notes.explanation: It is generally used to limit a loss or protect a profit on a stock sold short, which loses as the price rises.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC), Investor Bulletin “Understanding Order Types” (updated 18 August 2026), “Stop Order”
notes.evidence: A buy stop order is entered at a stop price above the current market price. Investors generally use a buy stop order to limit a loss or to protect a profit on a stock that they have sold short.

notes.front: A sell stop order is entered at a stop price {{c1::below}} the current market price.
notes.explanation: It is generally used to limit a loss or protect a profit on a stock the investor owns, which loses as the price falls.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC), Investor Bulletin “Understanding Order Types” (updated 18 August 2026), “Stop Order”
notes.evidence: A sell stop order is entered at a stop price below the current market price. Investors generally use a sell stop order to limit a loss or to protect a profit on a stock that they own.

notes.front: Is the stop price the guaranteed execution price of a stop order?
notes.back: No. It is only a trigger; the resulting market order can fill well away from it.
notes.explanation: Once triggered, the order is simply a market order.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC), Investor Bulletin “Understanding Order Types” (updated 18 August 2026), “Stop Order”
notes.evidence: The stop price is not the guaranteed execution price for a stop order. The stop price is a trigger that causes the stop order to become a market order.

notes.front: Ravi owns a stock now at $50. He wants to sell if it drops to $45, but refuses to accept less than $44. Which order fits?
notes.back: A: a sell stop-limit, stop $45, limit $44.
notes.choices:
A) Sell stop-limit: stop $45, limit $44
B) Sell stop at $45
C) Sell limit at $45
notes.choicesExplained: B: a stop order becomes a market order and could fill below $44. C: a sell limit at $45 would fill at once, since $50 is above $45.
notes.explanation: Once the stop price is reached, a stop-limit becomes a limit order, giving him control over the price.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC), Investor Bulletin “Stop, Stop-Limit, and Trailing Stop Orders” (updated 18 August 2026), “Stop-Limit Order”
notes.evidence: Once the stop price is reached, a stop-limit order becomes a limit order that will be executed at a specified price (or better). The benefit of a stop-limit order is that the investor can control the price at which the order can be executed.

notes.front: Kofi has sold a stock short at $30. He wants protection if it climbs past $34. Which order is generally used?
notes.back: A: a buy stop order at $34.
notes.choices:
A) A buy stop order at $34
B) A sell stop order at $34
C) A sell limit order at $34
notes.choicesExplained: B: sell stops protect stock you own, and sit below the market. C: selling more would add to his short position.
notes.explanation: A buy stop, set above the market, is generally used to limit a loss on a stock sold short.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC), Investor Bulletin “Stop, Stop-Limit, and Trailing Stop Orders” (updated 18 August 2026), “Stop Order”
notes.evidence: A buy stop order is entered at a stop price above the current market price. Investors generally use a buy stop order in an attempt to limit a loss or to protect a profit on a stock that they have sold short.

notes.front: Lee enters a limit order on Monday without choosing any time frame. It does not fill that day. What is its status on Tuesday?
notes.back: A: it has expired.
notes.choices:
A) It has expired
B) It is still working until cancelled
C) It has become a market order
notes.choicesExplained: B: only a GTC order lasts until executed or cancelled. C: nothing turns a limit order into a market order.
notes.explanation: Without a time frame an order is a day order, good only on the day it is entered; unfilled day orders do not carry over.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC), Investor Bulletin “Understanding Order Types” (updated 18 August 2026), “Day” and “Good-Til-Canceled (GTC)”
notes.evidence: Day orders, if not executed, generally cancel at the end of regular trading hours of the trading day that they are entered and will not carry over to the extended hours session or the next trading day.

notes.front: Under SEC Rule 15c1-7, what trading in a discretionary account is a manipulative, deceptive or fraudulent device?
notes.back: Transactions excessive in size or frequency given the account’s financial resources and character.
notes.explanation: The rule applies where the firm or its employee holds discretionary power over the account.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.15c1-7 (Rule 15c1-7, discretionary accounts), eCFR, paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: is vested with any discretionary power any transactions or purchase or sale which are excessive in size or frequency in view of the financial resources and character of such account

notes.front: A registered rep, holding written authority from the client, buys 100 shares for the client without contacting her first. How must the order be recorded?
notes.back: A: designated as discretionary.
notes.choices:
A) Designated as a discretionary order
B) As an ordinary client-instructed order
C) No order record is needed
notes.choicesExplained: B: the client did not instruct this trade; the rep exercised discretionary authority. C: every order needs a memorandum.
notes.explanation: SEC record rules require an order entered by exercising discretionary authority to be designated as such.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.17a-3 (Rule 17a-3, records to be made by certain exchange members, brokers and dealers), eCFR, paragraph (a)(6)
notes.evidence: An order entered pursuant to the exercise of discretionary authority by the member, broker or dealer, or associated person thereof, must be so designated.

notes.front: The bid price will almost always be {{c1::lower}} than the ask price.
notes.explanation: Buyers bid below what sellers ask, and that gap is the spread.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Bid Price”
notes.evidence: The bid price will almost always be lower than the ask or “offer,” price.

notes.front: When a firm acting as principal buys a security from you below the market price, the difference is called a {{c1::markdown}}.
notes.explanation: A markdown is the mirror of a markup: the principal’s pay built into the price when it buys rather than sells.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Markups and Markdowns”
notes.evidence: or by buying the security from you at a price that is lower than the market price (the difference is called a markdown).

notes.front: What must a trade confirmation say about the capacity in which the broker-dealer acted?
notes.back: Whether it acted as agent (for you, another person or both) or as principal for its own account.
notes.explanation: SEC Rule 10b-10 makes capacity part of the written notice to the customer.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.10b-10 (Rule 10b-10, confirmation of transactions), eCFR, paragraph (a)(2)
notes.evidence: Whether the broker or dealer is acting as agent for such customer, as agent for some other person, as agent for both such customer and some other person, or as principal for its own account

notes.front: A firm sells Jo a corporate bond out of its own inventory, at a price above the market price. In what capacity did it act, and how was it paid?
notes.back: A: principal, paid through a markup.
notes.choices:
A) Principal; a markup
B) Agent; a commission
C) Agent; a markup
notes.choicesExplained: B: an agent arranges a trade for you and charges a commission; here the firm sold its own bond. C: a markup is how a principal, not an agent, is paid.
notes.explanation: Selling from its own inventory makes the firm a principal, compensated by the price above market.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Markups and Markdowns”
notes.evidence: When a broker-dealer buys from or sells to you directly securities it holds in its own inventory, the broker-dealer acts as a principal in the transaction.

notes.front: Ken’s broker buys 100 shares for him from another investor on an exchange and charges him a separate fee for doing so. Capacity and pay?
notes.back: A: agent, paid a commission.
notes.choices:
A) Agent; a commission
B) Principal; a markup
C) Principal; a commission
notes.choicesExplained: B: the firm did not sell from its own inventory. C: a commission is the agent’s pay, not the principal’s.
notes.explanation: Arranging the trade on Ken’s behalf is acting as his agent, and the commission is the agent’s compensation.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Commissions”
notes.evidence: The commission compensates the financial professional and his or her firm when it is acting as agent for you in your securities transaction.

notes.front: How is a short sale normally settled, and how is it later closed out?
notes.back: Settled by delivering borrowed stock; closed by buying shares and returning them to the lender.
notes.explanation: The short seller never owned the shares, so borrowed ones are delivered and later replaced.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC), “Stock Purchases and Sales: Long and Short”, “Short Sales”
notes.evidence: Short sales are normally settled by the delivery of a security borrowed by or on behalf of the investor. The investor later closes out the position by returning the borrowed security to the stock lender, typically by purchasing securities on the open market.

notes.front: Under the SEC’s short-sale rules, what must a broker-dealer have before accepting a short sale order in an equity security?
notes.back: Borrowed the security, arranged to borrow it, or reasonable grounds to believe it can be borrowed for delivery.
notes.explanation: The rule ties short selling to the ability to deliver shares on the date delivery is due.
notes.source: 17 CFR 242.203 (Rule 203 of the SEC short-sale rules, borrowing and delivery requirements), eCFR, paragraph (b)(1)
notes.evidence: unless the broker or dealer has: (i) Borrowed the security, or entered into a bona-fide arrangement to borrow the security; or (ii) Reasonable grounds to believe that the security can be borrowed so that it can be delivered on the date delivery is due

notes.front: Nia does not own any shares of Acme but expects the price to fall. Which position lets her profit from that view?
notes.back: A: a short sale.
notes.choices:
A) A short sale
B) A long position
C) A buy limit order
notes.choicesExplained: B: a long position profits when the price rises. C: buying is a long position too.
notes.explanation: Short sellers believe the price will fall; if it drops they can buy back lower and profit.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Short Sales”
notes.evidence: Investors who sell short believe the price of the stock will fall. If the price drops, you can buy the stock at the lower price and make a profit.

notes.front: Besides betting on a fall, what can short selling be used to hedge?
notes.back: The risk of an economic long position in the same security or a related one.
notes.explanation: Market makers and others use short sales this way, as well as to provide liquidity.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC), “Stock Purchases and Sales: Long and Short”, “Short Sales”
notes.evidence: Short selling is also used by market makers and others to provide liquidity in response to unanticipated demand, or to hedge the risk of an economic long position in the same security or in a related security.

notes.front: Grace owns shares at $60 and wants to limit her loss if the price slides. Which order is generally used for this?
notes.back: A: a sell stop order below the market.
notes.choices:
A) A sell stop order below the market price
B) A buy stop order above the market price
C) A buy limit order
notes.choicesExplained: B: buy stops protect short positions. C: buying more adds to her exposure rather than limiting a loss.
notes.explanation: A sell stop is generally used to limit a loss or protect a profit on a stock the investor owns.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC), Investor Bulletin “Stop, Stop-Limit, and Trailing Stop Orders” (updated 18 August 2026), “Stop Order”
notes.evidence: Investors generally use a sell stop order in an attempt to limit a loss or to protect a profit on a stock that they own.

notes.front: Generally, a bull market is a rise of {{c1::20% or more}} in a broad market index over at least a two-month period.
notes.explanation: The yardstick is a broad index, not a single stock, over at least two months.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Bull Market”
notes.evidence: Generally, a bull market occurs when there is a rise of 20% or more in a broad market index over at least a two-month period.

notes.front: Tom expects Acme’s price to fall. How is his view described, and what might he do?
notes.back: A: bearish; he might sell it short.
notes.choices:
A) Bearish; sell it short
B) Bullish; buy it
C) Bearish; buy more
notes.choicesExplained: B: bullish means expecting a rise. C: buying profits from a rise, not a fall.
notes.explanation: Short sellers believe the price will fall, which is a bearish view.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Short Sales”
notes.evidence: Short sellers believe the price of the stock will fall, or are seeking to hedge against potential price volatility in securities that they own.

notes.front: Which component of return does a bondholder receive during the life of the bond?
notes.back: Interest, at a specified rate.
notes.explanation: The issuer promises interest during the bond’s life and repayment of principal at maturity.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Bonds”
notes.evidence: In return, the issuer promises to pay you a specified rate of interest during the life of the bond and to repay the principal, also known as face value or par value of the bond

notes.front: Which component of return is a portion of a company’s profit paid to shareholders?
notes.back: Dividends.
notes.explanation: Public companies that pay them usually do so on a fixed schedule, though special dividends can come at any time.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Dividend”
notes.evidence: A portion of a company's profit paid to shareholders. Public companies that pay dividends usually do so on a fixed schedule although they can issue them at any time.

notes.front: Which component of return comes from selling an investment for more than you paid?
notes.back: A capital gain.
notes.explanation: The gain is the profit over the price paid, and it arises when the investment is sold.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Capital Gain”
notes.evidence: The profit that comes when an investment is sold for more than the price the investor paid for it.

notes.front: Once nondividend distributions (return of capital) have cut your basis to zero, how are further ones treated?
notes.back: As capital gains.
notes.explanation: Reaching zero basis is the point where these distributions switch to reportable capital gain.
notes.source: IRS, Publication 550, Investment Income and Expenses, chapter 1, “Nondividend Distributions”
notes.evidence: When the basis of your stock has been reduced to zero, report any additional nondividend distribution you receive as a capital gain.

notes.front: A capital gain on an asset held {{c1::more than one year}} is generally long-term; held one year or less, it is short-term.
notes.explanation: The holding period decides the class: exactly one year still counts as short-term.
notes.source: IRS, Topic no. 409, Capital gains and losses, “Short-term or long-term”
notes.evidence: Generally, if you hold the asset for more than one year before you dispose of it, your capital gain or loss is long-term. If you hold it one year or less, your capital gain or loss is short-term.

notes.front: Ana bought shares at $30. They now trade at $45 and she still holds them. What kind of gain does she have?
notes.back: A: an unrealized gain.
notes.choices:
A) Unrealized
B) Realized
C) Return of capital
notes.choicesExplained: B: a gain is realized when the asset is sold. C: a return of capital is a distribution of her investment by the company.
notes.explanation: A capital gain is measured when you sell; until then the rise is only on paper.
notes.source: IRS, Topic no. 409, Capital gains and losses, “Capital gains and losses”
notes.evidence: When you sell a capital asset, the difference between the adjusted basis in the asset and the amount you realized from the sale is a capital gain or a capital loss.

notes.front: Stock dividends are generally not taxable; what is one case that makes one taxable?
notes.back: Any shareholder can choose cash or other property instead of the stock (among other cases).
notes.explanation: A cash option is one of the conditions the IRS lists that make such a distribution taxable.
notes.source: IRS, Publication 550, Investment Income and Expenses, chapter 1, “Taxable stock dividends and stock rights”
notes.evidence: You or any other shareholder have the choice to receive cash or other property instead of stock or stock rights.

notes.front: Eve’s 100 shares have a total basis of $3,300. She receives a nontaxable dividend of 10 identical shares. What is her basis per share now?
notes.back: A: $30 ($3,300 over 110 shares).
notes.choicesExplained: B: ignores the 10 new shares. C: divides by 1,000 shares rather than 110.
notes.explanation: The original basis is spread across all the shares now held.
notes.source: IRS, Publication 550, Investment Income and Expenses, chapter 4, “Stock dividends”
notes.evidence: If the new stock you received as a nontaxable dividend is identical to the old stock on which the dividend was declared, divide the adjusted basis of the old stock by the number of shares of old and new stock.

notes.front: If you cannot identify which shares you sold, whose basis do you use?
notes.back: The basis of the shares you acquired first.
notes.explanation: Without adequate identification, the earliest purchases are treated as sold first.
notes.source: IRS, Publication 550, Investment Income and Expenses, chapter 4, “Identification not possible”
notes.evidence: If you buy and sell securities at various times in varying quantities and you cannot adequately identify the shares you sell, the basis of the securities you sell is the basis of the securities you acquired first.

notes.front: For a covered security, what should your broker’s Form 1099-B show, and what is a covered security generally?
notes.back: Your basis; covered securities are generally those acquired after 2010, with exceptions.
notes.explanation: Brokers report basis on covered securities, which helps the investor complete Form 8949.
notes.source: IRS, Publication 550, Investment Income and Expenses, chapter 4, “Form 1099-B”
notes.evidence: If you sold a covered security in 2025, your broker should send you a Form 1099-B that shows your basis. This will help you complete Form 8949. Generally, a covered security is a security you acquired after 2010, with certain exceptions.

notes.front: Kay buys 200 shares at $25 each and pays a $20 commission. What is her cost basis?
notes.choicesExplained: B: leaves out the commission, a cost of purchase. C: subtracts the commission instead of adding it.
notes.explanation: Basis is the purchase price plus the costs of purchase, such as commissions.
notes.source: IRS, Publication 550, Investment Income and Expenses, chapter 4, “Stocks and Bonds”
notes.evidence: The basis of stocks or bonds you own is generally the purchase price plus the costs of purchase, such as commissions and recording or transfer fees.

notes.front: For a bond bought at a premium, is its yield to maturity above or below its coupon rate?
notes.back: Below the coupon rate.
notes.explanation: It is the premium price that pulls the yield to maturity below the coupon rate.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC), Investor Bulletin “What Are Corporate Bonds?”, Bond C
notes.evidence: Because of the premium price, the yield to maturity on Bond C at 2.84% is lower than the coupon rate.

notes.front: For a bond bought at a discount, is its yield to maturity above or below its coupon rate?
notes.back: Above the coupon rate.
notes.explanation: The buyer pays less than face value yet still gets the full coupons and face value at maturity.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC), Investor Bulletin “What Are Corporate Bonds?”, Bond B
notes.evidence: Bond B's price is 90% of its face value, or $900. Notwithstanding this, investors in Bond B will still receive a total of $40 per year in coupon payments and when Bond B matures, bondholders will still receive the face value of $1,000. The discounted price results in Bond B having a yield to maturity of 5.31%.

notes.front: A bond’s yield moves {{c1::inversely}} with its price.
notes.explanation: Price moves opposite to market interest rates, like a seesaw, and yield moves opposite to price.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC), Investor Bulletin “What Are Corporate Bonds?”, “What’s the relationship among bond prices, interest rates and yield?”
notes.evidence: The price of a bond moves in the opposite direction than market interest rates—like opposing ends of a seesaw. When interest rates go up, the price of the bond goes down. And when interest rates go down, the bond's price goes up. As shown above, a bond's yield also moves inversely with the bond's price.

notes.front: Lin holds a fixed-rate bond. Market rates then rise above its coupon. What tends to happen to its price, and to its yield to maturity for a new buyer?
notes.back: A: price falls and a new buyer’s YTM rises.
notes.choices:
A) Price falls; YTM for a new buyer rises
B) Price rises; YTM for a new buyer falls
C) Price and YTM both rise
notes.choicesExplained: B: that happens when rates fall. C: price and yield move inversely, so they do not rise together.
notes.explanation: The bond competes with new, higher-paying bonds, so its price falls and the yield for anyone buying it rises.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC), Investor Bulletin “What Are Corporate Bonds?”, “What’s the relationship among bond prices, interest rates and yield?”
notes.evidence: The price of the 3% bond may be more likely to fall. The yield to maturity for any new buyer, however, will rise as the price falls.

notes.front: A customer buys a callable bond quoted at a 5.2% yield to call; its yield to maturity is 4.9%. What must the confirmation show?
notes.back: A: both yields.
notes.choices:
A) Both the 5.2% yield to call and the 4.9% yield to maturity
B) Only the 5.2% yield to call
C) Only the 4.9% yield to maturity
notes.choicesExplained: B: the lower yield to maturity must also be shown. C: the represented yield, here yield to call, is shown as well.
notes.explanation: The rule stops a customer seeing only the higher of two yields.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.10b-10 (Rule 10b-10, confirmation of transactions), eCFR, paragraph (a)(6)(iii)
notes.evidence: If effected on a basis other than yield to maturity and the yield to maturity is lower than the represented yield, the yield to maturity as well as the represented yield

notes.front: A bond’s yield rises from 4.10% to 4.35%. By how many basis points has it risen?
notes.back: A: 25 basis points.
notes.choices:
A) 25 basis points
B) 2.5 basis points
C) 250 basis points
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: each basis point is 0.01 of a percentage point, so a 0.25-point rise is 25, not 2.5 or 250.
notes.explanation: One basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point, so 0.25 percentage points is 25 basis points.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Basis Point”
notes.evidence: One one-hundredth (.01) of a percentage point. For example, eight percent is equal to 800 basis points.

notes.front: An investor wants a benchmark made up of 30 “blue chip” American company stocks. Which index fits?
notes.back: A: the Dow Jones Industrial Average.
notes.choices:
A) The Dow Jones Industrial Average
B) The Wilshire 5000 Index
C) The Standard and Poor’s 500 Index
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Wilshire 5000 covers most publicly traded American stocks. C: the source lists it as a separate index from the 30-stock Dow.
notes.explanation: The source describes the Dow Jones Industrial Average as an index of 30 “blue chip” American company stocks; the Wilshire 5000 includes most publicly traded American stocks.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Market Indices”
notes.evidence: U.S. examples include the Dow Jones Industrial Average, an index of 30 "blue chip" U.S. company stocks, the Standard and Poor's 500 Index, and the Wilshire 5000 Index, which includes most publicly traded U.S. stocks.

notes.front: The ex-dividend date for stocks is usually the record date, or one business day {{c1::before}} if the record date is not a business day.
notes.explanation: The ex-date usually coincides with the record date.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Ex-Dividend Dates: When Are You Entitled to Stock and Cash Dividends”
notes.evidence: The ex-dividend date for stocks is usually set as the record date or one business day before if the record date is not a business day.

notes.front: If you buy a stock on its ex-dividend date, who receives the next dividend?
notes.back: The seller.
notes.explanation: Buying on or after the ex-date misses the dividend; buying before it gets it.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Ex-Dividend Dates: When Are You Entitled to Stock and Cash Dividends”
notes.evidence: If you purchase a stock on its ex-dividend date or after, you will not receive the next dividend payment. Instead, the seller gets the dividend. If you purchase before the ex-dividend date, you get the dividend.

notes.front: Besides dividends, what else does a company use its record date for?
notes.back: Deciding who is sent proxy statements, financial reports and other information.
notes.explanation: The same list of holders of record serves several company mailings.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Ex-Dividend Dates: When Are You Entitled to Stock and Cash Dividends”
notes.evidence: Companies also use this date to determine who is sent proxy statements, financial reports, and other information.

notes.front: When a dividend is 25% or more of the stock’s value, when is the ex-dividend date?
notes.back: Deferred until one business day after the dividend is paid.
notes.explanation: Special rules apply to such large dividends, overriding the usual record-date approach.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Ex-Dividend Dates: When Are You Entitled to Stock and Cash Dividends”, “Special Dividends”
notes.evidence: If the dividend is 25% or more of the stock value, special rules apply to the determination of the ex-dividend date. In these cases, the ex-dividend date will be deferred until one business day after the dividend is paid.

notes.front: If you sell before a stock dividend’s ex-date, what must you deliver, and what document covers it?
notes.back: The extra dividend shares go to the buyer; the seller receives an I.O.U. or “due bill” for them.
notes.explanation: Selling before the ex-date also sells the right to the stock dividend.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Ex-Dividend Dates: When Are You Entitled to Stock and Cash Dividends”, “Special Dividends”
notes.evidence: Your sale includes an obligation to deliver any shares acquired as a result of the dividend to the buyer of your shares, since the seller will receive an I.O.U. or "due bill" from his or her broker for the additional shares.

notes.front: A company sets a record date that falls on a Wednesday, a normal business day. Gita buys the stock that Wednesday. Does she get the dividend?
notes.back: A: no, Wednesday is the ex-date.
notes.choices:
A) No; the ex-date is that Wednesday
B) Yes; she is a holder on the record date
C) Yes, but only half of it
notes.choicesExplained: B: when the record date is a business day, the ex-date is usually the same day, and buyers on the ex-date miss the dividend. C: there is no partial entitlement.
notes.explanation: The ex-date is usually the record date itself when that is a business day, and buying on the ex-date misses the payment.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Ex-Dividend Dates: When Are You Entitled to Stock and Cash Dividends”
notes.evidence: The ex-dividend date for stocks is usually set as the record date or one business day before if the record date is not a business day. If you purchase a stock on its ex-dividend date or after, you will not receive the next dividend payment.

notes.front: Under SEC Rule 15c6-1, what is the standard (regular-way) settlement deadline for most broker-dealer trades?
notes.back: No later than the first business day after the trade date (T+1), unless the parties expressly agree otherwise.
notes.explanation: The rule bars contracts providing for payment and delivery later than that, unless both sides agree otherwise at the time of the trade.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.15c6-1 (Rule 15c6-1, settlement cycle), eCFR, paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: provides for payment of funds and delivery of securities later than the first business day after the date of the contract unless otherwise expressly agreed to by the parties at the time of the transaction

notes.front: Which three kinds of security, among others, does Rule 15c6-1(a) leave outside its T+1 requirement?
notes.back: Any three, among others: government securities, municipal securities, commercial paper, bankers’ acceptances, commercial bills, exempted securities.
notes.explanation: The rule names these in a parenthesis, so their settlement is not governed by its one-business-day limit.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.15c6-1 (Rule 15c6-1, settlement cycle), eCFR, paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: (other than an exempted security, a government security, a municipal security, commercial paper, bankers' acceptances, or commercial bills)

notes.front: Which sales may settle as late as the second business day under Rule 15c6-1(c)?
notes.back: Cash sales in a registered firm-commitment offering priced after 4:30 p.m. Eastern Time, to the underwriter or an initial purchaser.
notes.explanation: For these sales the limit is the second business day after the contract, unless otherwise agreed.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.15c6-1 (Rule 15c6-1, settlement cycle), eCFR, paragraph (c)
notes.evidence: contracts for the sale for cash of securities that are priced after 4:30 p.m. Eastern Time (ET) on the date such securities are priced and that are sold by an issuer to an underwriter pursuant to a firm commitment underwritten offering

notes.front: Lena buys listed shares on a Tuesday (no holidays that week). By when must the trade settle under the regular-way cycle?
notes.back: A: Wednesday, the first business day after the trade date.
notes.choices:
A) Wednesday
B) Thursday
C) Tuesday
notes.choicesExplained: B: that would be two business days, the old T+2 cycle. C: same-day settlement is not the standard cycle.
notes.explanation: Rule 15c6-1 requires settlement no later than the first business day after the date of the contract.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.15c6-1 (Rule 15c6-1, settlement cycle), eCFR, paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: provides for payment of funds and delivery of securities later than the first business day after the date of the contract

notes.front: Marco sells listed shares on a Friday (Monday is not a holiday). On which day does the trade settle regular way?
notes.back: A: Monday, the next business day.
notes.choices:
A) Monday
B) Saturday
C) Tuesday
notes.choicesExplained: B: Saturday is not a business day. C: Tuesday would be two business days after the trade.
notes.explanation: The deadline counts business days, so the first business day after a Friday is the Monday.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.15c6-1 (Rule 15c6-1, settlement cycle), eCFR, paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: provides for payment of funds and delivery of securities later than the first business day after the date of the contract

notes.front: What cost can holding a paper certificate bring that book-entry avoids?
notes.back: The expense of replacing it if you lose it.
notes.explanation: Book-entry records ownership without any certificate to lose.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Holding Your Securities”
notes.evidence: If you lose the certificate, you will incur expenses to replace it. Alternative approaches eliminate the need to hold certificates by relying on a “book-entry” record of ownership.

notes.front: Is an investor holding shares in street name a registered owner or a beneficial owner?
notes.back: A beneficial owner: the shares are held indirectly, for example through a broker-dealer.
notes.explanation: Holding indirectly, through an intermediary, is what makes the owner beneficial.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Beneficial Owner”
notes.evidence: A beneficial owner holds stocks indirectly, for example, through a bank or broker-dealer. Beneficial owners are sometimes said to be holding shares in "street name."

notes.front: Does a stock split dilute existing shareholders’ ownership?
notes.back: No. Unlike issuing new shares, a split does not dilute ownership.
notes.explanation: The contrast is with issuing new shares, which can dilute existing holders.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Stock Split”
notes.evidence: Unlike issuing new shares, a stock split does not dilute the ownership interests of existing shareholders.

notes.front: Owen holds 300 shares trading at $90 when the company declares a 3-for-1 split. What does he hold just after the split?
notes.back: A: 900 shares at about $30.
notes.choices:
A) 900 shares at about $30
B) 100 shares at about $270
C) 900 shares at about $90
notes.choicesExplained: B: that is a reverse split. C: a split adds shares without adding value, so the price falls.
notes.explanation: A split increases the number of shares without changing shareholders’ equity, so the price per share falls in step.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Stock Split”
notes.evidence: For example, if you own 100 shares of a company that trades at $100 per share and the company declares a two-for-one stock split, you will own 200 shares at $50 per share immediately after the split.

notes.front: Hana bought 100 shares for $4,000 in total. The company splits 2-for-1. What is her basis per share afterwards?
notes.back: A: $20 a share ($4,000 over 200 shares).
notes.choicesExplained: B: that ignores the new shares. C: that doubles instead of halving.
notes.explanation: IRS rules figure split basis like a stock dividend of identical stock: the old basis is divided over old and new shares.
notes.source: IRS, Publication 550, Investment Income and Expenses, chapter 4, “Stock splits”
notes.evidence: Figure the basis of stock splits in the same way as stock dividends if identical stock is distributed on the stock held.

notes.front: Why might a company declare a reverse stock split?
notes.back: To raise its share price, for example to regain an exchange’s minimum bid price.
notes.explanation: The aim is a higher trading price, for example when it is thought too low to attract investors.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Reverse Stock Splits”
notes.evidence: A company may declare a reverse stock split in an effort to increase the trading price of its shares – for example, when it believes the trading price is too low to attract investors to purchase shares, or in an attempt to regain compliance with minimum bid price requirements of an exchange on which its shares trade.

notes.front: In some reverse stock splits, what happens to small shareholders?
notes.back: They are cashed out for their fractional shares and no longer own the company’s shares.
notes.explanation: A holding smaller than one new share can only become a fraction, which may be paid in cash.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Reverse Stock Splits”
notes.evidence: In some reverse stock splits, small shareholders are "cashed out" (receiving a proportionate amount of cash in lieu of partial shares) so that they no longer own the company’s shares.

notes.front: Priti owns 4,000 shares. The company does a 1-for-8 reverse split. How many shares does she own afterwards?
notes.back: A: 500 shares.
notes.choicesExplained: B: that multiplies, as a forward split would. C: a reverse split changes the share count.
notes.explanation: Each old share becomes one-eighth of a new share.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Reverse Stock Splits”
notes.evidence: For example, if a company declares a one for ten reverse stock split, every ten shares that you own will be converted into a single share.

notes.front: What does SEC Rule 10b-18 give an issuer that repurchases its own common stock?
notes.back: A voluntary safe harbour from manipulation liability, if its manner, timing, price and volume conditions are met.
notes.explanation: Compliance is voluntary; it shields the issuer only from liability arising from how, when and how much it buys.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.10b-18 (Rule 10b-18, purchases of certain equity securities by the issuer and others), eCFR, Preliminary note 1
notes.evidence: provides an issuer (and its affiliated purchasers) with a “safe harbor” from liability for manipulation under sections 9(a)(2) of the Act and § 240.10b-5 under the Act solely by reason of the manner, timing, price, and volume of their repurchases

notes.front: Company Q offers every holder the chance, for a limited time, to sell it up to 15% of Q’s own shares at a price above market. What is this?
notes.back: A: an issuer tender offer.
notes.choices:
A) An issuer tender offer
B) A third-party tender offer
C) A stock split
notes.choicesExplained: B: in a third-party offer an outsider buys another company’s securities. C: a split changes the share count; nothing is bought.
notes.explanation: Who the buyer is decides the label.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Tender Offer”
notes.evidence: A tender offer where the company seeks to acquire its own securities is often referred to as an issuer tender offer. A tender offer where a third party seeks to acquire another company’s securities is referred to as a third party tender offer.

notes.front: A tender offer’s purchase price is usually at a {{c1::premium to the current market price}}.
notes.explanation: The premium is there to encourage holders to sell.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Tender Offer”
notes.evidence: The purchase price is usually at a premium to the current market price of the securities in order to encourage security holders to sell their securities.

notes.front: Under SEC Rule 14e-1, what is the minimum period a tender offer must stay open?
notes.back: Twenty business days from when it is first published or sent to holders.
notes.explanation: Holding it open less time is treated as a fraudulent, deceptive or manipulative practice under section 14(e).
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.14e-1 (Rule 14e-1, unlawful tender offer practices), eCFR, paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: Hold such tender offer open for less than twenty business days from the date such tender offer is first published or sent to security holders

notes.front: What are two protections SEC rules give holders in most tender offers?
notes.back: Any two: withdrawal rights; the offer open to all holders of the class; best price for every tendering holder.
notes.explanation: These rules stop a bidder treating holders differently or locking them in.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Tender Offer”
notes.evidence: These protections include: “withdrawal rights,” which is the right of security holders to withdraw their tender of securities within certain time periods; the requirement that the tender be open to all holders of the class of securities subject to the offer; and, the bidder’s obligation to provide each tendering holder with the “best price,”

notes.front: Which investor protection is missing from a mini-tender offer?
notes.back: Withdrawal rights (bidders need not provide them, nor file documents with the SEC).
notes.explanation: An investor who tenders into such an offer cannot change their mind and take the shares back.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Mini-Tender Offers”
notes.evidence: Bidders making mini-tender offers also do not have to file documents with the SEC or provide withdrawal rights to investors who tender their shares into the offer.

notes.front: May an offeror solicit tenders in an exchange offer before its registration statement is effective?
notes.back: Yes, but it may buy no securities until the registration is effective and the offer has expired.
notes.explanation: Rule 162 lets the offer start early while holding back the purchase itself.
notes.source: 17 CFR 230.162 (Rule 162, submission of tenders in registered exchange offers), eCFR, paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: an offeror may solicit tenders of securities in an exchange offer before a registration statement is effective as to the security offered, so long as no securities are purchased until the registration statement is effective and the tender offer has expired

notes.front: Leo receives rights to buy more of a company’s stock at a set price, but he does not want more shares. The rights have a market value. What can he do?
notes.back: A: sell them (or let them expire).
notes.choices:
A) Sell the rights, or let them expire
B) Nothing; he must exercise them
C) Return them to the company for their full value
notes.choicesExplained: B: exercising is only one option. C: the source gives no such option.
notes.explanation: A right to acquire stock can be used, traded or left to lapse.
notes.source: IRS, Publication 550, Investment Income and Expenses, chapter 4, “Stock rights”
notes.evidence: A stock right is a right to acquire a corporation's stock. It may be exercised, it may be sold if it has a market value, or it may expire.

notes.front: Typically, a merger must be approved by the holders of a {{c1::majority of the outstanding shares}} of the target company.
notes.explanation: The vote that typically decides it is that of the target company’s outstanding shares.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Mergers”
notes.evidence: Typically, a merger must be approved by the holders of a majority of the outstanding shares of the target company.

notes.front: Iris owns shares in a company being taken over for cash. She thinks the price is unfair. What may state law give her, and what is the catch?
notes.back: A: appraisal or dissenter’s rights, if procedures are followed precisely.
notes.choices:
A) Appraisal or dissenter’s rights, lost unless she follows the procedures precisely
B) An automatic right to a higher price
C) The right to block the merger on her own
notes.choicesExplained: B: nothing is automatic; the rights must be pursued. C: approval typically needs a majority of the target’s outstanding shares, not one holder.
notes.explanation: The merger documents explain these rights and their deadlines.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Mergers”
notes.evidence: If you believe the amount you will receive is not fair, check these documents for information on appraisal or dissenter's rights under state law. You must follow the procedures precisely or your appraisal or dissenter’s rights may be lost.

notes.front: How soon must a broker-dealer forward proxy materials it receives to its customers who are beneficial owners?
notes.back: No later than five business days after receiving them.
notes.explanation: The five-day clock runs from the broker’s receipt of the materials.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.14b-1 (Rule 14b-1, obligations of registered brokers and dealers in connection with the prompt forwarding of certain communications), eCFR, paragraph (b)(2)
notes.evidence: forward such materials to its customers who are beneficial owners of the registrant's securities no later than five business days after receipt of the proxy material, information statement or annual report to security holders

notes.front: Uma holds shares in street name and ignores the proxy for a routine matter at the annual meeting. What may happen to her shares’ vote?
notes.back: A: her broker may vote them at its discretion.
notes.choices:
A) Her broker may vote them at its discretion
B) They cannot be voted at all
C) The company votes them for management
notes.choicesExplained: B: for routine matters brokers may cast uninstructed votes. C: the discretion belongs to the broker, not the company.
notes.explanation: These are called uninstructed or discretionary broker votes.
notes.source: Investor.gov (SEC) glossary, “Broker Vote”
notes.evidence: For certain routine matters to be voted upon at shareholder meetings, if you don’t vote by proxy or at the meeting in person, brokers may vote on your behalf at their discretion.
